t: Count the Number of Beautiful Subarrays — Prefix XOR Parity
o: An operation removes the same power of two from two elements, which flips that bit off in both — it preserves the XOR parity structure: a subarray can be zeroed exactly when the XOR of all its elements is 0 (each bit appears an even number of times). So we must count subarrays with XOR 0. Example 1: [4,3,1,2,4] has XOR 0 overall and [3,1,2] has XOR 0 → 2 subarrays. Example 2: every prefix XOR is nonzero and distinct → 0. Classic technique: count pairs of equal prefix XORs with a hash map; n up to 1e5 forces O(n).
k: The operation cancels equal bits pairwise, so a subarray is beautiful iff its XOR is 0.
Subarray (l..r] has XOR 0 iff prefixXor[l] == prefixXor[r]; count such pairs with a frequency map seeded with {0:1}.

a.i: Maintain a running XOR and a map from XOR value to occurrences among prefixes seen so far. Each new prefix contributes the count of earlier equal prefixes as newly found beautiful subarrays ending here.
s: Initialize map {0:1}, running xor x = 0, answer 0.
For each element: x ^= v; add map[x] to answer; increment map[x].

c.python:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
    def beautifulSubarrays(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        cnt = defaultdict(int)
        cnt[0] = 1
        x = ans = 0
        for v in nums:
            x ^= v
            ans += cnt[x]
            cnt[x] += 1
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average hash operations
a.sp: O(n) — the map holds at most n+1 distinct prefix XORs

w: Prove the XOR-zero characterization before coding: each operation removes 2^k from two numbers, preserving XOR mod 2 per bit, and repeated cancellation achieves zero iff every bit count is even. Pitfalls: returning int instead of 64-bit (answer up to ~n²/2 ≈ 5e9), and forgetting the seed {0:1}. Follow-up: count beautiful subarrays of length at least L, or in a mutable array (add a BIT over prefix XORs).
